stories.title: Vidact – a compiler that turns React into direct DOM operations
stories.author: mohebifar

topComments.author: mohebifar
topComments.text: I started Vidact as an experiment 6 years ago, an experimental compiler that takes React-style function components and hooks and compiles them into direct DOM operations. The basic idea is: keep React's programming model, but replace its runtime model. It was a very ambitious project back then, but recently, another project I was working on (grep.codemod.com) inspired me to rebuild this and I thought of using React compiler's analysis this time as it has already done most of the heavy lifting. With Vidact, a component runs once when it mounts. The compiler analyzes which expressions depend on which values and generates static update functions for them. When state changes, it directly updates the affected text node, attribute, conditional range, or list item. So instead of: state change -> rerender component -> create element tree -> reconcile -> mutate DOM it's closer to: state change -> run compiler-selected updater -> mutate DOM There is no Virtual DOM, no reconciler, no runtime dependency tracking, and React itself isn't shipped to the browser. The compiler is written in Rust and uses React Compiler's analysis infrastructure for AST/scope/HIR/CFG/SSA and dependency information, but Vidact has its own IR, DOM code generator, and runtime. I've also been experimenting with the same model for SSR/hydration and built Vidact Start around it, with file-based routes, loaders, SSR, hydration, and client navigation. One design decision I'm particularly interested in feedback on: Vidact fails compilation when it encounters React behavior it can't preserve rather than silently falling back to React or a slower runtime path. It's therefore intentionally a subset of React today. It's beta and there are definitely compatibility edges left to explore. I'm especially interested in cases where React semantics make static compilation fundamentally difficult, rather than just features I haven't implemented yet. Site: https://www.vidact.dev/ Source: https://github.com/mohebifar/vidact

topComments.author: dofm
topComments.text: > Our society does not support classical musicians in the same way that we support ‘popular’ musicians. It really really does. Popular/rock/folk/classical musicians all earn much the same way now: a blend of teaching, occasional performance fees, functions performances like weddings and galas, music-related side-gigs (composition, arrangement and recording for commercial music), and non-music-related side gigs — teaching non-musical things, gardening, painting and decorating, bar work, office temp work, even full time jobs (doctors and lawyers, accountants). I know a couple of classical musicians whose actual money-making music is playing other instruments in funk/rock functions bands. Even the "best" or most famous musicians, popular or classical, have side gigs. Approximately nobody makes their money only from performing or from recordings; that ended twenty-five or thirty years ago. Elite soloists, maybe — but that is actually a pretty expensive life to live. I would be surprised if many of them risked a life where they had no other job. The idea that a "conservatory" system exists that meaningfully supports classical musicians is nonsense almost anywhere in the world, I would think. Even the first-chair musicians and conductors have side gigs. (ETA: I can't believe this is a workable model for mathematicians, either. Maybe for a couple of dozen the world over. But there is no performance, no regionality, little in the way of public dissemination, little in the way of reflected glory for benefactors. No, the "conservatory" will perhaps be the intelligence agencies, as it was before.)

Does the current model (of highly-talented academics at Universities mostly arguing with each other) change because of AI? Does it invalidate human effort, or does it allow humans to push the boundaries further? Is there no point in training or paying for mathematicians because AI will take over the whole role? Or, as we're finding with so many other areas, does AI do its best work when guided by someone who knows the area and subject well?

If the address-of operator ( &var ) already yields the memory address of a variable, why did the design of C necessitate distinct pointer types/variables instead of operating directly with references or expressions like &var ? For example: int x = 10; // &x gives the address of x int *p = &x; // p stores the address From an architectural and compiler design standpoint: What core capabilities (such as dynamic memory allocation, argument passing, or data structure design) strictly require an address to be stored in an assignable variable rather than evaluated directly via & ? What would a language design look like—or fail to accomplish—if addresses were rvalues only and could not be stored in dedicated pointer variables?

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Splitting hand-drawn elements from a photographed paper background
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: We're building a Python pipeline that digitalises hand-drawn images by automatically detecting and extracting individual elements from smartphone photos as clean PNG cutouts with transparent backgrounds, preserving their original coordinates for reassembly. Our main challenge is reliable segmentation , which in our case means separating individual elements from each other and from the paper background - particularly when elements share similar colours, the paper has shadows and wrinkles, or handwritten text needs to be preserved separately. stackOverflowQuestions.title: Expo SwiftUI native view is positioned incorrectly inside React Native flexDirection: "row"
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I'm using Expo UI ( @expo/ui ) to create a custom native SwiftUI Liquid Glass wrapper for iOS 26. The wrapper itself works correctly: the Liquid Glass is always positioned correctly around its React Native child . The problem is specifically the position of the entire native SwiftUI wrapper inside a React Native horizontal flex layout . When the parent uses flexDirection: "column" , everything is positioned correctly. When the parent uses flexDirection: "row" , the child and its Liquid Glass are rendered correctly relative to each other, but the whole SwiftUI/Host view is positioned incorrectly within the row . For example: <View style={{ width: "100%", flexDirection: "row", alignItems: "center", justifyContent: "space-between", }} > <LiquidGlass matchContents> <Pressable onPress={onBack} style={styles.backButton}> <Text style={styles.backText}>Back</Text> </Pressable> </LiquidGlass> <Pressable onPress={onSubmit} style={styles.submitButton} > <Text style={styles.submitText}>Continue</Text> </Pressable> </View> The expected behavior is: ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ [ Liquid Glass / Back ] [ Continue ] │ │ │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘ But the native Liquid Glass wrapper is positioned incorrectly when the parent participates in the horizontal Yoga layout. Important distinction This is not a problem with the glass frame relative to its child . The relationship: LiquidGlassWrapper ↓ React Native child is correct. The problem is: React Native row ↓ LiquidGlassWrapper The native wrapper's position in the row is incorrect. Interestingly, changing the parent to: flexDirection: "column" makes the positioning work correctly. My implementation My React Native wrapper is: import { Host } from "@expo/ui/swift-ui"; import { RNHostView } from "@expo/ui"; import { LiquidGlassWrapper } from "@/modules/liquid-glass/src/LiquidGlassSwiftUIView"; import { LiquidGlassWrapperProps } from "@/modules/liquid-glass/src/LiquidGlass.types"; import
